lessons.0.slides.1.title: Why Producers Matter More Than in Other Regions
lessons.0.slides.1.content: Unlike Bordeaux — where the château system centralises ownership — Burgundy's highly fragmented land means that the same Grand Cru plot can be owned by dozens of producers, each making wildly different wine. Choosing the right producer is therefore more important than choosing the appellation.
lessons.0.slides.2.title: 🏆 Domaine de la Romanée-Conti (DRC)
lessons.0.slides.2.points.0: Undisputed world number one, no serious challenger
lessons.0.slides.2.points.1: Production approximately 6,000 cases per year; average bottle price above US$5,000
lessons.0.slides.2.points.2: Certified biodynamic; entirely estate-grown, harvested by hand
lessons.0.slides.2.points.3: Grand Cru monopoles: Romanée-Conti (1.8 ha) and La Tâche (6.1 ha)
lessons.0.slides.2.points.4: Other holdings: La Romanée-Saint-Vivant, Richebourg, Grands Échézeaux, Échézeaux
lessons.0.slides.2.points.5: White: Montrachet (0.67 ha); recent red: Corton
lessons.0.slides.2.points.6: Waiting lists of many years; allocation is the only route to purchase
lessons.0.slides.3.title: 👑 Domaine Leroy
lessons.0.slides.3.points.0: Founded by Lalou Bize-Leroy, a pioneer of biodynamic viticulture
lessons.0.slides.3.points.1: Extraordinarily low yields: 15–20 hl/ha (conventional average 40 hl/ha)
lessons.0.slides.3.points.2: Price second only to DRC; quality rivals or surpasses it
lessons.0.slides.3.points.3: Style: richness, purity, and remarkable ageing potential
lessons.0.slides.3.points.4: Holdings across Vosne-Romanée, Chambolle, Gevrey, and Pommard
lessons.0.slides.3.points.5: Available only through auction or specialist secondary market

lessons.0.slides.6.title: How to Find the Right Producer
lessons.0.slides.6.content: Read specialist critics (Burghound, Wine Advocate, Decanter). Follow auction results and secondary-market prices. Attend tastings and explore local importers. Note that the most famous names are the hardest to obtain — excellent alternatives exist at every price point.

lessons.1.title: Winemaking Philosophy and Style
lessons.1.slides.0.title: Winemaking Philosophy
lessons.1.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 2 - 20 minutes
lessons.1.slides.0.description: Understand the different philosophical approaches to making Burgundy
lessons.1.slides.1.title: Traditional vs. Modern Winemaking
lessons.1.slides.1.content: Burgundy's winemakers span a wide philosophical spectrum, from strict traditionalists who intervene as little as possible to modernists who use technology to achieve precision and consistency. Most great producers sit somewhere in the middle — respectful of tradition while open to useful innovation.
lessons.1.slides.2.title: 🌿 Biodynamic Viticulture
lessons.1.slides.2.points.0: Based on Rudolf Steiner's philosophy: treat the vineyard as a living ecosystem
lessons.1.slides.2.points.1: Use of natural preparations (horn manure, herbal sprays)
lessons.1.slides.2.points.2: Follow a lunar calendar for vineyard and cellar work
lessons.1.slides.2.points.3: Zero synthetic pesticides, herbicides, or fertilisers
lessons.1.slides.2.points.4: Leading practitioners: Leroy, Leflaive, Comte Armand, Comtes Lafon
lessons.1.slides.2.points.5: Studies suggest improved soil microbial health and pure terroir expression
lessons.1.slides.3.title: Organic vs. Biodynamic
lessons.1.slides.3.content: Organic = no synthetic chemicals. Biodynamic = organic principles plus cosmic cycles and special preparations. Pros: pure terroir expression, soil health, sustainability. Cons: disease management is harder, yields are lower, costs are higher. Trend: increasing adoption among top domaines.
lessons.1.slides.4.title: 🔑 Key Winemaking Decisions
lessons.1.slides.4.points.0: Whole-bunch vs. destemmed — whole bunches add spice, structure, and complexity
lessons.1.slides.4.points.1: Cold maceration — extracts fruit colour and aromatics before fermentation
lessons.1.slides.4.points.2: Fermentation temperature — too high (above 32 °C) destroys elegance
lessons.1.slides.4.points.3: Punch-down vs. pump-over — both extract colour and tannin differently
lessons.1.slides.4.points.4: New oak (0–100%) — shapes style; excess masks terroir
lessons.1.slides.4.points.5: Ageing duration (12–24 months) — allows integration of oak and tannin
lessons.1.slides.4.points.6: Filtration and fining — minimal intervention preserves texture
lessons.1.slides.5.title: 🏔️ Terroir Over Technique
lessons.1.slides.5.points.0: Consensus among top producers: winemaking serves terroir, not the reverse
lessons.1.slides.5.points.1: The best wines are made with minimum cellar intervention
lessons.1.slides.5.points.2: The vineyard is where great wine is made — the cellar is where it can be ruined
lessons.1.slides.5.points.3: Over-extraction, excessive oak, and heavy filtration erase terroir character
lessons.1.slides.5.points.4: Transparency: the winemaker's goal is to transmit, not transform
lessons.1.slides.5.points.5: This philosophy is why Burgundy wines age so gracefully

lessons.2.title: Rising Domaines and Future Trends
lessons.2.slides.0.title: Rising Domaines and Future Trends
lessons.2.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 3 - 23 minutes
lessons.2.slides.0.description: Discover Burgundy's emerging talents and understand where the region is heading
lessons.2.slides.1.title: The New Generation of Winemakers
lessons.2.slides.1.content: Over the past 20 years a wave of young winemakers has returned to family estates or founded new labels, bringing formal wine education alongside deep respect for tradition. Many have worked harvests abroad and returned with fresh perspectives.
lessons.2.slides.2.title: 🌟 Notable Emerging Domaines
lessons.2.slides.2.points.0: Sylvain Cathiard — Vosne-Romanée, intense and pure, now highly sought
lessons.2.slides.2.points.1: Thibault Liger-Belair — Nuits-Saint-Georges, reclaimed family vines, outstanding quality
lessons.2.slides.2.points.2: David Duband — Gevrey and Vosne, elegant and consistent
lessons.2.slides.2.points.3: Arnaud Mortet — Gevrey-Chambertin, excellent value for the appellation
lessons.2.slides.2.points.4: Benjamin Leroux — formerly Comte Armand; now independent, technically brilliant
lessons.2.slides.2.points.5: Alex Gambal — American transplant, meticulous négociant
lessons.2.slides.2.points.6: High quality, relatively accessible, and worthy of early investment
lessons.2.slides.3.title: 🌍 Future Trends
lessons.2.slides.3.points.0: Climate adaptation — later ripening varieties, higher-altitude sites
lessons.2.slides.3.points.1: Sustainability — move from conventional to organic/biodynamic
lessons.2.slides.3.points.2: Precision viticulture — drone mapping, satellite data, soil sensors
lessons.2.slides.3.points.3: Parcel sub-division — more single-vineyard bottlings within existing appellations
lessons.2.slides.3.points.4: Internationalisation — Burgundian producers and grapes appearing worldwide
lessons.2.slides.3.points.5: Price polarisation — top wines continue to rise; everyday Burgundy becomes better value
lessons.2.slides.3.points.6: New appellation development — Côte Chalonnaise gaining renewed attention
lessons.2.slides.4.title: 💰 Investment Strategy
lessons.2.slides.4.points.0: Classic estates (DRC, Leroy) — stable long-term value, liquid on secondary market
lessons.2.slides.4.points.1: Emerging domaines — growth potential, but choose carefully
lessons.2.slides.4.points.2: Undervalued regions — Côte Chalonnaise, Mâcon for quality-to-price
lessons.2.slides.4.points.3: Quality négociants — reasonable prices and good market liquidity
lessons.2.slides.4.points.4: Suggested allocation: 70% established classics, 30% emerging talent
lessons.2.slides.4.points.5: Hold for a minimum of 10–15 years to realise appreciation
lessons.2.slides.5.title: How to Discover Good Producers
lessons.2.slides.5.content: Don't follow critic scores blindly — taste for yourself. Read specialist press and follow reputable importers. Attend Burgundy tastings and Hospices de Beaune events. Visit the region: meeting winemakers builds trust and often opens allocation channels. Build your own taste standard. Ultimately, drink what you enjoy, not what others say you should.
